I have farmed these fields for over fifty years, and I know what works in Quzhou. My family has four mu of good land, and I cannot let it sit idle. This year, like every year, I will plant winter wheat in the autumn and then sow summer maize right after the wheat comes off in early June. That is the rotation our village has always followed, and it is the only way I know to feed my household.

For the wheat, I will buy improved seeds from the agro-shop in town. I will prepare the ground with the rotary tiller because my back is too old for heavy ploughing now. I will spread compound fertilizer as a base and top-dress with urea when the wheat greens up in spring. The crop needs three good irrigations: one before the cold sets in, one when the stems shoot up, and one when the grain fills. I will also spray for aphids, weeds, and the rust that always comes when the spring is damp. If the frost is not too cruel, I hope to harvest about five hundred kilograms from each mu.

After the wheat is threshed, I will plant hybrid maize seeds — the kind in the packets that give big, full ears. I will not till again; the machine plants straight into the wheat stubble to save time and fuel, which is what everyone does now. Maize needs less fuss than wheat: two irrigations should be enough if the summer rains come, and I will spray three times to keep the worms and weeds down. If the weather is fair, each mu should give me about five hundred and fifty kilograms.

That is my plan. It is what I have always done, and it puts food on the table.
